chapters.title: 19. Margarita
paragraphs: Follow me, reader! Who told you that there is no true, faithful, eternal love in this world? May the liar have his vile tongue cut out!
Follow me, my reader, and me alone, and I will show you such a love!

No! The master was mistaken when, in the hospital, at the hour when night was tipping over past midnight, he told Ivanushka bitterly that she had forgotten him. That could not be. Of course she had not forgotten him.

First of all, let us reveal the secret that the master did not wish to reveal to Ivanushka. His beloved’s name was Margarita Nikolayevna. Everything the master told the poor poet about her was the plain truth. He had described his beloved accurately. She was beautiful and clever. To this one more thing must be added: it can be said with confidence that many women would have given anything at all to exchange their lives for the life of Margarita Nikolayevna. Childless, thirty years old, Margarita was the wife of a very prominent specialist, a man who had, moreover, made a discovery of the utmost importance to the state. Her husband was young, handsome, kind, honest, and adored his wife. Margarita Nikolayevna and her husband, the two of them alone, occupied the whole upper floor of a beautiful private house set in a garden in one of the side streets near the Arbat. A charming place! Anyone can see this for themselves who cares to go to that garden. Let them apply to me, I will tell them the address and show them the way—the house is still standing to this day.

Margarita Nikolayevna did not need money. Margarita Nikolayevna could buy anything she liked. Among her husband’s acquaintances there were some interesting people. Margarita Nikolayevna never had to touch a primus stove. Margarita Nikolayevna did not know the horrors of living in a shared apartment. In short... was she happy? Not for a single minute! Ever since she had married at nineteen and come to live in the house, she had not known happiness. O gods, my gods! What, then, did this woman need?! What did this woman need, in whose eyes there always burned some strange little flame? What did she need, this witch with a slight cast in one eye, who had decked herself out with mimosa that spring? I do not know. It is unknown to me. Evidently she was telling the truth: she needed him, the master, and not at all the Gothic house, or the private garden, or the money. She loved him; she was telling the truth.

Even I, a truthful narrator but an outsider, feel my heart clench at the thought of what Margarita went through when she came to the master’s little house the next day—having, luckily, not managed to talk to her husband, who had not come back at the appointed time—and learned that the master was no longer there. She did everything she could to find out something about him and, of course, found out precisely nothing. Then she went back to the house and took up her life in the old place.

But as soon as the dirty snow had vanished from the pavements and roadways, as soon as the rotten, restless wind of spring began to blow in through the window vents, Margarita Nikolayevna began to pine even more than in winter. She often wept in secret, long and bitterly. She did not know whom she loved: a living man or a dead one? And the further the desperate days went on, the more often, especially at twilight, the thought came to her that she was bound to a dead man.

She had either to forget him or to die herself. One cannot drag out a life like that, after all. One cannot! Forget him, whatever it cost—forget him! But he would not be forgotten; that was the whole trouble.

“Yes, yes, yes, the very same mistake!” Margarita would say, sitting by the stove and gazing into the fire, lit in memory of the fire that had burned when he was writing Pontius Pilate. “Why did I leave him that night? Why? It was madness! I came back the next day, honestly, as I had promised, but it was already too late. Yes, I came back, like the unfortunate Levi Matvei, too late!”

All these words were, of course, absurd, because, really, what would have changed if she had stayed with the master that night? Would she have saved him? Ridiculous!—we would exclaim, but we shall not do so before a woman driven to despair.

On the very day when all that absurd commotion was going on, caused by the appearance of the black magician in Moscow—on Friday, when Berlioz’s uncle was chased back to Kiev, when the bookkeeper was arrested and a great many other utterly stupid and incomprehensible things took place—Margarita woke up around noon in her bedroom, whose bay window looked out from the turret of the house.

On waking, Margarita did not weep, as often happened, because she woke with a presentiment that today, at last, something was going to happen. Having felt this presentiment, she began to warm it and nurture it in her soul, fearful that it might leave her.

“I believe!” Margarita whispered solemnly. “I believe! Something is going to happen! It cannot not happen, because what, really, have I been sent this lifelong torment for? I confess that I lied and deceived and lived a secret life, hidden from people, but still, one cannot be punished so cruelly for that. Something is bound to happen, because nothing can drag on forever. And besides, my dream was prophetic, I can vouch for that.”
So Margarita Nikolayevna whispered, looking at the crimson curtains as they filled with sunlight, dressing restlessly, combing her short curled hair in front of the triple mirror.

The dream Margarita had dreamed that night really was unusual. The thing was that during her winter torments she had never once seen the master in her dreams. At night he left her alone, and she suffered only in the daytime hours. But now she had dreamed of him.

She dreamed of a place unknown to Margarita—hopeless, dismal, under the overcast sky of early spring. She dreamed of that ragged, scudding, grayish sky, and under it a soundless flock of rooks. Some gnarled little bridge, and under it a muddy spring stream. Joyless, beggarly, half-bare trees. A lone aspen, and further off, among the trees, beyond some sort of vegetable plot, a little log building—whether a separate kitchen, or a bathhouse, or the devil knows what. Everything around was somehow lifeless and so dismal that it simply made you want to hang yourself from that aspen by the little bridge. Not a breath of wind, not a stir of cloud, and not a living soul. Now there is a hellish place for a living person!

And then, imagine it, the door of that log building is flung open, and he appears. Quite far away, but clearly visible. He is in rags; you cannot make out what he is wearing. His hair is tousled, he is unshaven. His eyes are sick, alarmed. He beckons her with his hand, calls to her. Choking in the lifeless air, Margarita ran to him over the tussocks, and at that moment she woke up.

“This dream can mean only one of two things,” Margarita Nikolayevna reasoned with herself. “If he is dead and beckoned to me, that means he came for me, and I shall soon die. That would be very good, because then the torment will come to an end. Or else he is alive, and then the dream can mean only one thing: that he is reminding me of himself! He wants to say that we shall see each other again. Yes, we shall see each other very soon!”

Still in the same excited state, Margarita dressed and began to persuade herself that, in essence, everything was turning out very luckily, and that one must know how to seize such lucky moments and make use of them. Her husband had gone away on a business trip for three whole days. For three days and nights she was left to herself; no one would stop her thinking about whatever she pleased, dreaming about whatever she liked. All five rooms on the upper floor of the house, this whole apartment, which tens of thousands of people in Moscow would have envied, were entirely at her disposal.

Yet, having been given her freedom for three whole days, Margarita chose out of all this luxurious apartment a place that was far from the best. After drinking her tea, she went into a dark, windowless room where suitcases and assorted old things were kept in two large wardrobes. Squatting down, she opened the bottom drawer of the first of them and, from under a pile of silk remnants, took out the one thing of value she had in life. In Margarita’s hands was an old album of brown leather, which held a photograph of the master, a savings bank book with a deposit of ten thousand in his name, the petals of a dried rose pressed flat between sheets of tissue paper, and part of a full-sized notebook, typewritten and with its bottom edge burned.

Returning to her bedroom with these riches, Margarita Nikolayevna stood the photograph up against the three-leaved mirror and sat for about an hour holding the fire-damaged notebook on her knees, leafing through it and rereading what, after the burning, had neither beginning nor end: “...The darkness that came from the Mediterranean Sea covered the city the procurator hated. The hanging bridges joining the temple to the dreadful Antonia Tower vanished, an abyss descended from the sky and flooded the winged gods above the hippodrome, the Hasmonean palace with its loopholes, the bazaars, the caravanserais, the lanes, the pools... Yershalaim, the great city, was gone, as if it had never existed in the world...”
Margarita wanted to read on, but there was nothing further except an uneven charred fringe.

Wiping away her tears, Margarita Nikolayevna put the notebook aside, rested her elbows on the dressing table beneath the mirror and, reflected in the glass, sat for a long time without taking her eyes off the photograph. Then the tears dried. Margarita carefully put her possessions together, and a few minutes later they were buried once more under the silk rags, and in the dark room the lock clicked shut with a ring.

Margarita Nikolayevna was putting on her coat in the hall to go out for a walk. The beautiful Natasha, her housemaid, asked what to make for the main course and, on hearing that it did not matter, began, to amuse herself, a conversation with her mistress, telling her God knows what: that yesterday at the theater a conjurer had done such tricks that everyone gasped; he had handed out two bottles of foreign perfume and stockings to everyone free of charge, and then, when the show was over, the audience went out into the street and—bang—everyone turned out to be naked! Margarita Nikolayevna collapsed onto the chair under the mirror in the hall and roared with laughter.
“Natasha! Really, you ought to be ashamed of yourself,” Margarita Nikolayevna was saying. “You’re an educated, intelligent girl; people in queues tell the devil knows what lies, and you repeat them!”

Natasha flushed crimson and objected with great heat that it was not lies at all, and that only today, at the grocery on the Arbat, she had seen with her own eyes a certain citizen who had come into the shop in shoes, and as soon as she went to pay at the till, the shoes vanished from her feet and she was left standing in nothing but her stockings. Eyes popping, a hole in her heel! And those shoes were magic ones, from that very show.
“And she just went off like that?”

“Just like that!” Natasha cried out, blushing more and more because she was not believed. “And last night, Margarita Nikolayevna, the police picked up about a hundred people. Women citizens from that show were running down Tverskaya in nothing but their knickers.”
“Well, of course, it was Darya who told you this,” Margarita Nikolayevna was saying. “I noticed long ago that she’s a terrible liar.”

The funny conversation ended with a pleasant surprise for Natasha. Margarita Nikolayevna went into the bedroom and came out holding a pair of stockings and a bottle of eau de cologne. Telling Natasha that she, too, wanted to perform a trick, Margarita Nikolayevna presented her with both the stockings and the bottle and said that she asked only one thing of her: not to run down Tverskaya in nothing but her stockings, and not to listen to Darya. After kissing each other, the mistress and the housemaid parted.

Leaning back against the comfortable, soft back of her seat in the trolleybus, Margarita Nikolayevna rode along the Arbat, now thinking her own thoughts, now listening to what two citizens sitting in front of her were whispering about.

And they, glancing round warily now and then in case anyone was listening, were whispering about some nonsense. A strapping, fleshy one with lively piggy little eyes, sitting by the window, was quietly telling his small neighbor that they had had to close the coffin with a black cloth...
“It can’t be!” the small one whispered, astounded. “That’s unheard of... And what did Zheldybin do?”
Amid the even hum of the trolleybus came words from the window seat:
“Criminal investigation... a scandal... sheer mysticism, that’s what it is!”

From these scraps Margarita Nikolayevna somehow pieced together something coherent. The citizens were whispering that from some dead man—which one they did not say—the head had been stolen out of the coffin that morning! That was why this Zheldybin was so upset now. And the two who were whispering in the trolleybus also had some connection with the robbed dead man.
“Will we have time to stop for flowers?” the small one fretted. “The cremation’s at two, you said?”
At last Margarita Nikolayevna grew tired of listening to this mysterious drivel about a head stolen from a coffin, and she was glad that it was time for her to get off.
A few minutes later Margarita Nikolayevna was already sitting under the Kremlin wall on one of the benches, placed so that she could see the Manege.

Margarita squinted at the bright sun, remembering her dream of that night, remembering how exactly a year ago, to the day and to the hour, she had sat on this very same bench beside him. And exactly as then, her black handbag lay beside her on the bench. He was not beside her that day, but in her thoughts Margarita Nikolayevna was talking to him all the same: “If you have been exiled, then why don’t you let me know about yourself? People do let others know. Have you stopped loving me? No, for some reason I don’t believe that. Then you were exiled and you died... In that case, I beg you, let me go, give me freedom at last to live, to breathe the air!” Margarita Nikolayevna answered herself on his behalf: “You are free... Am I holding you?” Then she retorted to him: “No, what kind of answer is that? No, you leave my memory, and then I shall be free.”

People walked past Margarita Nikolayevna. A certain man gave the well-dressed woman a sidelong glance, drawn by her beauty and her solitude. He coughed and sat down on the very end of the same bench on which Margarita Nikolayevna was sitting. Summoning up his courage, he began:
“Decidedly fine weather today...”
But Margarita gave him such a gloomy look that he got up and left.

“There’s an example for you,” Margarita said in her mind to the one who possessed her. “Why, exactly, did I drive that man away? I’m bored, and there’s nothing bad about this Lovelace, unless it’s that stupid word ‘decidedly’? Why am I sitting alone under the wall like an owl? Why am I shut out of life?”

She grew quite sad and hung her head. But then, suddenly, that same morning wave of expectation and excitement pushed at her breast. “Yes, it will happen!” The wave pushed at her a second time, and then she realized that it was a wave of sound. Through the noise of the city, the approaching beats of a drum and the sounds of slightly out-of-tune trumpets could be heard more and more distinctly.

First to appear was a mounted policeman riding at a walk past the garden railings, and behind him three on foot. Then a slowly moving truck with musicians. After that, a slowly moving new, open funeral car, on it a coffin covered in wreaths, and at the corners of the platform four people standing: three men and one woman.

Even at a distance Margarita could make out that the faces of the people standing in the funeral car, accompanying the dead man on his last journey, were somehow strangely bewildered. This was especially noticeable in the case of the woman citizen standing in the left rear corner of the hearse. This citizen’s fat cheeks seemed to be puffed out even further from within by some piquant secret, and ambiguous little lights played in her puffy little eyes. It seemed that any moment now, just a little more, and the citizen, unable to hold out, would wink toward the dead man and say: “Have you ever seen anything like it? Sheer mysticism!” The mourners on foot, about three hundred of them, who walked slowly behind the funeral car, had equally bewildered faces.

Margarita followed the procession with her eyes, listening as the dismal Turkish drum faded in the distance, beating out the same “boom, boom, boom,” and thought: “What a strange funeral... And what misery there is in that ‘boom’! Ah, truly, I would pawn my soul to the devil just to find out whether he is alive or not?.. I wonder who it is they’re burying with such astonishing faces?”
“Mikhail Alexandrovich Berlioz,” came a somewhat nasal male voice beside her, “chairman of Massolit.”

Surprised, Margarita Nikolayevna turned and saw on her bench a citizen who had evidently sat down noiselessly while Margarita was absorbed in watching the procession and had, it must be supposed, absentmindedly asked her last question out loud.
Meanwhile the procession had begun to slow to a halt, probably held up ahead by traffic lights.
“Yes,” the unknown citizen went on, “they’re in an astonishing mood. They’re carrying a dead man, and all they can think about is where his head has got to!”

“What head?” asked Margarita, peering at her unexpected neighbor. This neighbor turned out to be short, fiery red-haired, with a fang, in starched linen, a good-quality striped suit, patent-leather shoes, and with a bowler hat on his head. His tie was garish. The astonishing thing was that from the breast pocket, where men usually carry a handkerchief or a fountain pen, this citizen had a gnawed chicken bone sticking out.
“Well, you see, if you please,” the red-haired man explained, “this morning in the hall at Griboyedov’s somebody pinched the dead man’s head out of the coffin.”
“But how can that be?” Margarita asked involuntarily, remembering at the same time the whispering in the trolleybus.

“The devil knows how!” the red-haired man answered breezily. “Though I suppose it wouldn’t hurt to ask Behemoth about it. Swiped it terribly deftly. Such a whopping scandal! And the main thing is, it’s incomprehensible who needs it and what for, that head!”
Preoccupied as Margarita Nikolayevna was with her own affairs, she was nevertheless struck by the unknown citizen’s strange lies.
“Excuse me!” she suddenly exclaimed. “What Berlioz? The one who was in the papers today...”
“That’s the one, that’s the one...”
“So, then, those are writers walking behind the coffin?” asked Margarita, and suddenly bared her teeth.
“Well, naturally, it’s them!”
“And do you know them by sight?”
“Every last one of them,” answered the red-haired man.
“Tell me,” Margarita began, and her voice grew hollow, “isn’t the critic Latunsky among them?”
“How could he not be?” answered the red-haired man. “There he is, at the end of the fourth row.”
“The blond one, you mean?” asked Margarita, squinting.
“Ash-colored... See, he’s raised his eyes to heaven.”
“Looks like a priest?”
“That’s it, that’s it!”
Margarita asked nothing more, gazing intently at Latunsky.
“And you, as I can see,” the red-haired man said, smiling, “hate this Latunsky.”
“There are a few others I hate as well,” Margarita answered through her teeth, “but that’s not interesting to talk about.”
Meanwhile the procession moved on, and behind the mourners on foot came a string of cars, for the most part empty.
“Yes, indeed, of course, what’s interesting about it, Margarita Nikolayevna!”
Margarita was surprised:
“You know me?”
Instead of answering, the red-haired man took off his bowler and held it out at arm’s length with a flourish.
“A perfect cutthroat’s mug!” thought Margarita, peering at her street companion.
“But I don’t know you,” Margarita said drily.
“How could you know me? And yet I have been sent to you on a little matter of business.”
Margarita turned pale and recoiled.
“You should have started with that straight away,” she began, “instead of babbling the devil knows what about a severed head! Do you want to arrest me?”
“Nothing of the sort,” exclaimed the red-haired man. “What is all this: as soon as a man starts talking, it has to be an arrest! I simply have a matter of business with you.”
“I don’t understand a thing. What business?”
The red-haired man looked round and said mysteriously:
“I was sent to invite you to pay a visit this evening.”
“What are you raving about, what visit?”
“To a certain very distinguished foreigner,” the red-haired man said significantly, narrowing one eye.
Margarita was very angry.
“A new breed has appeared: the street pimp!” she said, getting up to leave.
“Well, thanks very much for errands like this!” the red-haired man exclaimed, offended, and grumbled at the back of the departing Margarita: “Fool!”
“Scoundrel!” she retorted, turning round, and immediately heard the red-haired man’s voice behind her:

“The darkness that came from the Mediterranean Sea covered the city the procurator hated. The hanging bridges joining the temple to the dreadful Antonia Tower vanished... Yershalaim, the great city, was gone, as if it had never existed in the world... So go to perdition, then, you and your burned notebook and your dried rose! Sit here on the bench alone and beg him to let you go free, to let you breathe the air, to leave your memory!”
Her face gone white, Margarita came back to the bench. The red-haired man was looking at her with narrowed eyes.

“I don’t understand anything,” Margarita Nikolayevna began quietly. “About the pages, one could still find out... get in, spy on me... Natasha has been bribed, is that it? But how could you know my thoughts?” She winced in anguish and added: “Tell me, who are you? What office are you from?”
“What a bore,” the red-haired man grumbled, and then spoke louder: “Excuse me, but I told you I’m not from any office at all! Sit down, please.”
Margarita obeyed without a word, but still, as she sat down, she asked once more:
“Who are you?”
“All right, then, my name is Azazello, but that won’t mean anything to you anyway.”
“And you won’t tell me how you found out about the pages and about my thoughts?”
“I will not,” Azazello answered drily.
“But do you know something about him?” Margarita whispered imploringly.
“Well, let’s say I do.”
“I beg you, tell me just one thing: is he alive? Don’t torment me!”
“Well, he’s alive, he’s alive,” Azazello responded reluctantly.
“God!”
“Please, no agitation and no shrieking,” said Azazello, frowning.

“Forgive me, forgive me,” muttered Margarita, submissive now. “Of course, I was angry with you. But you must agree, when a woman is invited somewhere on the street to pay a visit... I have no prejudices, I assure you”—Margarita smiled joylessly—“but I never see any foreigners, I have no wish whatever to associate with them... and besides, my husband... My drama is that I live with a man I don’t love, but I consider it unworthy to spoil his life. I have never had anything but kindness from him...”
Azazello listened to this incoherent speech with visible boredom and said sternly:
“I’ll ask you to be quiet for one moment.”
Margarita fell silent obediently.
“I am inviting you to a foreigner who is perfectly safe. And not a single soul will know of this visit. That I can vouch for, at least.”
“And what does he want me for?” Margarita asked insinuatingly.
“You will find that out later.”
“I see... I am to give myself to him,” Margarita said thoughtfully.
To this Azazello gave a sort of haughty grunt and answered thus:
“Any woman in the world, I can assure you, would dream of it”—Azazello’s mug twisted into a smirk—“but I shall disappoint you: that will not happen.”
“What sort of foreigner is he?!” Margarita exclaimed in confusion, so loudly that people walking past the bench turned to look at her. “And what interest do I have in going to him?”
Azazello leaned toward her and whispered meaningfully:
“Well, now, the interest is a very great one... You will take advantage of the opportunity...”
“What?” exclaimed Margarita, and her eyes grew round. “If I understand you correctly, you are hinting that I may find out about him there?”
Azazello nodded silently.
“I’ll go!” Margarita exclaimed with force, and seized Azazello by the hand. “I’ll go anywhere you like!”
Puffing with relief, Azazello leaned back against the back of the bench, covering with his back the word “Nyura,” carved into it in big letters, and began ironically:

“They’re a difficult lot, these women!” He thrust his hands into his pockets and stretched his legs far out in front of him. “Why, for instance, was I sent on this job? Behemoth should have gone, he’s charming...”
Margarita began, smiling crookedly and bitterly:

“Stop mystifying me and tormenting me with your riddles... I am an unhappy person, after all, and you are taking advantage of it. I am getting myself into some strange business, but I swear, only because you lured me with words about him! My head is spinning from all these incomprehensible things...”

“No dramas, no dramas,” Azazello responded, grimacing. “You must try to see my position too. Punching an administrator in the mug, or throwing an uncle out of the house, or shooting somebody, or some other trifle of that kind—that’s my proper specialty, but talking to women in love—no, thank you very much! I’ve been coaxing you for half an hour now. So, are you going?”
“I am going,” Margarita Nikolayevna answered simply.

“Then kindly take this,” said Azazello, and taking a round gold box out of his pocket, he held it out to Margarita with the words: “Do hide it, passers-by are looking. It will come in handy, Margarita Nikolayevna; you’ve aged a good deal from grief over the last six months.” Margarita flushed but made no reply, and Azazello went on: “This evening, at exactly half past nine, kindly strip naked and rub this ointment over your face and your whole body. After that, do whatever you like, but don’t go far from the telephone. At ten I will ring you and tell you everything you need to know. You will not have to worry about anything; you will be taken where you need to go, and you will not be put to any inconvenience. Understood?”
Margarita was silent for a while, then answered:
“Understood. This thing is pure gold, you can tell by the weight. Well, then, I understand perfectly well that I am being bribed and drawn into some shady business for which I shall pay dearly.”
“What’s all this?” Azazello almost hissed. “You’re at it again?..”
“No, wait!”
“Give back the cream!”
Margarita clutched the box more tightly in her hand and went on:

“No, wait... I know what I’m getting into. But I’m going into everything for his sake, because I have no other hope of anything left in the world. But I want to tell you that if you destroy me, you will be ashamed! Yes, ashamed! I am perishing for love!” And, striking her breast, Margarita looked up at the sun.
“Give it back,” Azazello shouted in a fury, “give it back, and to the devil with the whole thing! Let them send Behemoth!”

“Oh, no!” exclaimed Margarita, astonishing the passers-by. “I agree to everything, I agree to go through this comedy of rubbing in the ointment, I agree to go to the devil’s own back of beyond! I won’t give it back!”
“Ba!” Azazello suddenly bellowed and, goggling at the garden railings, began pointing at something with his finger.

Margarita turned to where Azazello was pointing but found nothing special there. Then she turned back to Azazello, wishing to get an explanation of this absurd “Ba!”, but there was no one to give the explanation: Margarita Nikolayevna’s mysterious companion had vanished.

Margarita quickly thrust her hand into her handbag, where she had hidden the box just before that shout, and made sure it was there. Then, without stopping to think about anything, Margarita hurried out of the Alexander Garden at a run.

chapters.title: 20. Azazello’s Cream
paragraphs: The moon hung full in the clear evening sky, visible through the branches of a maple. The lindens and acacias had painted the ground in the garden with an intricate pattern of patches. The three-paned window in the bay, open but with the curtain drawn across it, glowed with a furious electric light. In Margarita Nikolayevna’s bedroom every light was burning, illuminating the complete disorder of the room.

On the bed, on top of the blanket, lay chemises, stockings and underwear, while crumpled underwear simply lay about on the floor beside a box of cigarettes crushed in the excitement. Shoes stood on the bedside table next to an unfinished cup of coffee and an ashtray in which a cigarette end was smoking. A black evening dress hung over the back of a chair. The room smelled of perfume. Besides that, the smell of a hot iron drifted into it from somewhere.

Margarita Nikolayevna sat in front of the pier glass in nothing but a bathrobe thrown over her naked body and black suede shoes. A gold bracelet with a little watch lay in front of Margarita Nikolayevna, next to the box she had received from Azazello, and Margarita could not take her eyes off the dial. At times it began to seem to her that the watch had broken and the hands were not moving. But they were moving, although very slowly, as if sticking, and at last the long hand dropped onto the twenty-ninth minute past nine. Margarita’s heart gave a terrible thump, so that she could not even pick up the box straight away. Mastering herself, Margarita opened it and saw in the box a rich yellowish cream. It seemed to her that it smelled of marsh slime. With the tip of her finger Margarita put a small dab of the cream on her palm, at which the smell of marsh grasses and forest grew stronger, and then with her palm she began rubbing the cream into her forehead and cheeks.

The cream spread easily and, as it seemed to Margarita, evaporated at once. After rubbing it in a few times, Margarita glanced in the mirror and dropped the box right onto the glass of the watch, which cracked all over. Margarita closed her eyes, then looked once more and burst into wild laughter.

Her eyebrows, plucked at the edges into a thin thread with tweezers, had thickened and lay in even black arches over eyes that had turned green. The thin vertical crease cutting across the bridge of her nose, which had appeared back in October when the master vanished, had disappeared without a trace. Gone, too, were the yellowish shadows at her temples and the two barely noticeable webs of fine lines at the outer corners of her eyes. The skin of her cheeks was suffused with an even pink, her forehead had become white and clear, and the hairdresser’s waves in her hair had come undone.
Out of the mirror, at the thirty-year-old Margarita, there looked a naturally curly, black-haired woman of about twenty, laughing uncontrollably and baring her teeth.

Having laughed her fill, Margarita leaped out of the bathrobe in a single bound, scooped up a large handful of the light, rich cream and with vigorous strokes began rubbing it into the skin of her body. It at once turned pink and began to glow. Then instantly, as if a needle had been plucked out of her brain, the temple that had ached all evening since the meeting in the Alexander Garden grew quiet, the muscles of her arms and legs grew stronger, and then Margarita’s body lost its weight.
She gave a little jump and hung in the air not far above the carpet, then she was slowly drawn downward, and she came down.
“What a cream! What a cream!” cried Margarita, throwing herself into an armchair.

The rubbing had changed her not only outwardly. Now, all through her, in every particle of her body, joy was bubbling up, and she felt it as tiny bubbles prickling her whole body. Margarita felt herself free, free of everything. Besides, she understood with complete clarity that the very thing had happened that her presentiment had spoken of that morning, and that she was leaving the house and her former life forever. But from that former life one thought had still broken off and stayed with her: that she had only to fulfill one last duty before the beginning of something new and extraordinary that was drawing her upward, into the air. And, naked as she was, she ran from the bedroom, every now and then flying up into the air, into her husband’s study and, putting on the light, rushed to the desk. On a sheet torn from a notepad she quickly wrote a note in pencil, in large letters, without a single correction:

“Forgive me and forget me as soon as you can. I am leaving you forever. Do not look for me, it is useless. I have become a witch from the grief and misfortunes that have struck me. It is time for me to go. Farewell.
Margarita”

With a completely lightened heart, Margarita flew back into the bedroom, and right after her Natasha ran in, loaded with things. And at once all these things—a wooden hanger with a dress, lace handkerchiefs, blue silk shoes on shoe trees, and a belt—all of it went tumbling to the floor, and Natasha clasped her freed hands together.
“Well, am I lovely?” Margarita Nikolayevna shouted loudly in a hoarse voice.
“How can this be?” whispered Natasha, backing away. “How do you do it, Margarita Nikolayevna?”
“It’s the cream! The cream, the cream!” answered Margarita, pointing at the gleaming gold box and turning this way and that in front of the mirror.

Natasha, forgetting the crumpled dress lying on the floor, ran up to the pier glass and stared with greedy, kindled eyes at what was left of the ointment. Her lips were whispering something. She turned to Margarita again and said, with a kind of reverence:
“Your skin, eh? Your skin! Margarita Nikolayevna, your skin is glowing!” But then she came to her senses, ran over to the dress, picked it up and began shaking it out.

“Leave it! Leave it!” Margarita shouted to her. “To the devil with it, leave it all! No, wait—take it for yourself as a keepsake. I mean it, take it as a keepsake. Take everything there is in the room!”
As though she had lost her wits, Natasha stood motionless, looking at Margarita for some time, then hung on her neck, kissing her and crying:
“Like satin! It glows! Like satin! And your eyebrows, your eyebrows!”
“Take all the rags, take the perfume, and drag them off to your trunk, hide them,” Margarita shouted, “but don’t take the jewels, or they’ll accuse you of theft!”
Natasha gathered up into a bundle whatever came to hand—dresses, shoes, stockings and underwear—and ran out of the bedroom.

At that moment, from somewhere on the other side of the lane, out of an open window, a thunderous, virtuoso waltz burst forth and came flying, and there was the puffing of a car pulling up at the gate.
“Azazello is about to ring!” exclaimed Margarita, listening to the waltz pouring out over the lane. “He will ring! And the foreigner is safe. Yes, now I understand that he is safe!”
The car roared as it drove away from the gate. The wicket gate banged, and footsteps sounded on the flagstones of the path.
“That’s Nikolai Ivanovich, I know him by his step,” thought Margarita. “I must do something very funny and interesting by way of farewell.”

Margarita jerked the curtain aside and sat sideways on the windowsill, clasping her knee with her hands. The moonlight licked her right side. Margarita raised her head to the moon and put on a pensive and poetic face. The footsteps tapped twice more and then suddenly stopped. After admiring the moon a little longer and sighing for propriety’s sake, Margarita turned her head toward the garden and indeed saw Nikolai Ivanovich, who lived on the ground floor of this same house. The moon was flooding Nikolai Ivanovich with bright light. He was sitting on a bench, and everything about him showed that he had sunk onto it suddenly. The pince-nez on his face had somehow gone askew, and he was clutching his briefcase in his hands.
“Ah, hello, Nikolai Ivanovich,” Margarita said in a sad voice, “good evening! Coming from a meeting?”
Nikolai Ivanovich made no reply to this.
“And I,” Margarita went on, leaning further out into the garden, “am sitting here alone, as you see, bored, looking at the moon and listening to the waltz.”
Margarita passed her left hand over her temple, smoothing a strand of hair, then said crossly:
“That’s impolite, Nikolai Ivanovich! I am a lady, after all, when all’s said and done! It’s downright boorish not to answer when someone is speaking to you!”

Nikolai Ivanovich, visible in the moonlight down to the last little button on his gray waistcoat, down to the last hair of his fair, wedge-shaped little beard, suddenly smirked a wild smirk, rose from the bench and, evidently beside himself with embarrassment, instead of taking off his hat, swung his briefcase out to the side and bent his knees, as though he were about to break into a squatting dance.

“Oh, what a boring type you are, Nikolai Ivanovich!” Margarita went on. “Altogether, I’m so sick of all of you that I can’t express it to you, and I am so happy to be parting with you! To the devil’s mother with the lot of you!”
At that moment, behind Margarita’s back, the telephone burst out ringing in the bedroom. Margarita tore herself off the windowsill and, forgetting Nikolai Ivanovich, seized the receiver.
“Azazello speaking,” said the receiver.
“Dear, dear Azazello!” cried Margarita.

“It’s time! Fly out,” Azazello began on the line, and from his tone one could hear that he was pleased by Margarita’s sincere, joyful outburst. “When you fly over the gate, shout ‘Invisible!’ Then fly about over the city for a bit to get used to it, and after that south, out of the city, and straight to the river. You are expected!”

Margarita hung up, and at that moment something in the next room began hobbling woodenly and banging against the door. Margarita flung it open, and a floor brush, bristles up, came dancing into the bedroom. Its end beat a drum roll on the floor; it kicked and strained toward the window. Margarita squealed with delight and leaped astride the brush. Only then did the thought flash through the rider’s mind that in all this fuss she had forgotten to get dressed. She galloped over to the bed and grabbed the first thing that came to hand, some pale blue chemise. Waving it like a standard, she flew out of the window. And the waltz over the garden struck up louder.

From the window Margarita slid down and saw Nikolai Ivanovich on the bench. He seemed frozen to it and, utterly stunned, was listening to the shouts and crashing coming from the lighted bedroom of the upstairs tenants.
“Farewell, Nikolai Ivanovich!” shouted Margarita, capering in front of Nikolai Ivanovich.
He gasped and crawled along the bench, groping his way along it with his hands and knocking his briefcase to the ground.

“Farewell forever! I’m flying away!” shouted Margarita, drowning out the waltz. Here she realized that she had no use whatever for the chemise and, with a sinister laugh, threw it over Nikolai Ivanovich’s head. Blinded, Nikolai Ivanovich crashed from the bench onto the bricks of the path.
Margarita turned to take a last look at the house where she had suffered for so long, and in the blazing window she saw Natasha’s face, distorted with amazement.

“Farewell, Natasha!” shouted Margarita, and jerked the brush up. “Invisible! Invisible!” she shouted even louder, and between the maple branches, which lashed her across the face, she flew over the gate and out into the lane. And after her flew the waltz, now gone completely mad.

chapters.title: 21. Flight
paragraphs: Invisible and free! Invisible and free! Flying down her own lane, Margarita found herself in another that crossed the first at a right angle. This patched, darned, crooked and long lane, with the lopsided door of a paraffin shop where they sell kerosene by the mug and insecticide in little bottles, she cut across in a single instant, and here she learned that even when one is completely free and invisible, one must still be at least a little sensible, even in delight. Only by braking through some miracle did she avoid smashing herself to death against an old lopsided lamppost on the corner. Swerving round it, Margarita gripped the brush more tightly and flew more slowly, peering at the electric wires and the signs hanging across the pavement.

The third lane led straight to the Arbat. Here Margarita fully mastered the steering of the brush, understood that it obeyed the slightest touch of her hands or feet, and that when flying over the city one must be very attentive and not run too wild. Besides, it had become perfectly clear back in the lane that the passers-by could not see the flier. Nobody threw back their head, nobody shouted “Look, look!”, nobody leaped aside, squealed or fainted, or laughed with wild laughter.

Margarita flew soundlessly, very slowly and not high, at about the level of the second floor. But even flying slowly, right at the mouth of the dazzlingly lit Arbat, she misjudged slightly and struck her shoulder against some illuminated disk with an arrow painted on it. This made Margarita angry. She reined in the obedient brush, flew off to one side, and then, hurling herself at the disk without warning, smashed it to smithereens with the end of the brush. The fragments rained down with a crash, the passers-by leaped aside, somewhere a whistle blew, and Margarita, having committed this unnecessary act, burst out laughing. “On the Arbat I must be even more careful,” thought Margarita. “There’s such a tangle of everything here that you can’t make any sense of it.” She began diving between the wires. Beneath Margarita floated the roofs of trolleybuses, buses and cars, and along the pavements, as it seemed to Margarita from above, floated rivers of caps. From these rivers little streams branched off and poured into the fiery maws of the night shops.

“Ugh, what a mess!” Margarita thought angrily. “You can’t turn round here.” She crossed the Arbat, rose higher, to the level of the fourth floors, and, past the dazzlingly shining tubes on the corner building of the theater, floated into a narrow lane of tall buildings. All the windows in them were open, and from every window came radio music. Out of curiosity Margarita looked into one of them. She saw a kitchen. Two primus stoves were roaring on the range, and beside them stood two women with spoons in their hands, squabbling.

“You have to turn off the light after yourself in the lavatory, that’s what I’m telling you, Pelageya Petrovna,” said the woman in front of whom stood a saucepan of some sort of food that was pouring out steam, “or else we’ll apply to have you evicted!”
“You’re a fine one yourself,” answered the other.

“You’re both fine ones,” Margarita said resonantly, tumbling over the windowsill into the kitchen. Both the quarreling women turned toward the voice and froze with their dirty spoons in their hands. Margarita carefully stretched out her hand between them, turned the taps on both primus stoves and put them out. The women gasped and their mouths fell open. But Margarita had already grown bored in the kitchen and flew out into the lane.

At the end of it her attention was caught by the sumptuous bulk of an eight-story building, evidently just built. Margarita went down and, landing, saw that the facade of the building was faced with black marble, that the doors were wide, that behind their glass could be seen a doorman’s cap with gold braid and his buttons, and that above the doors was inscribed in gold: “Dramlit House.”

Margarita squinted at the inscription, trying to work out what the word “Dramlit” might mean. Taking the brush under her arm, Margarita walked into the entrance, bumping the astonished doorman with the door, and saw on the wall beside the lift a huge black board, and on it, written out in white letters, the numbers of the apartments and the surnames of the tenants. The heading that crowned the list, “House of the Dramatist and Man of Letters,” made Margarita let out a predatory, stifled howl. Rising higher in the air, she began greedily reading the surnames: Khustov, Dvubratsky, Kvant, Beskudnikov, Latunsky...
“Latunsky!” Margarita shrieked. “Latunsky! Why, that’s him... He’s the one who destroyed the master!”
The doorman by the door, his eyes bulging and even hopping with astonishment, stared at the black board, trying to understand such a miracle: why had the list of tenants suddenly shrieked?
And Margarita by this time was already rushing up the stairs, repeating in a kind of rapture:
“Latunsky—eighty-four... Latunsky—eighty-four...”
There on the left—82, on the right—83, higher still, on the left—84. Here! And there was the card: “O. Latunsky.”

Margarita jumped off the brush, and the stone landing pleasantly cooled her hot soles. Margarita rang once, twice. But no one opened. Margarita began pressing the button harder and could hear for herself the jangling it set up in Latunsky’s apartment. Yes, the occupant of apartment No. 84 on the eighth floor should be grateful to the late Berlioz to the end of his days for the chairman of Massolit having fallen under a tram, and for the memorial meeting having been fixed for precisely that evening. The critic Latunsky was born under a lucky star. It saved him from a meeting with Margarita, who had become a witch that Friday.

No one opened. Then Margarita raced downward at full tilt, counting the floors, reached the bottom, burst out into the street and, looking up, counted and checked the floors from the outside, working out which windows exactly were those of Latunsky’s apartment. Undoubtedly they were the five dark windows at the corner of the building, on the eighth floor. Having made sure of this, Margarita rose into the air, and a few seconds later she was entering, through an open window, an unlit room in which only a narrow path of moonlight shone silver. Margarita ran along it and groped for the switch. A minute later the whole apartment was lit up. The brush stood in a corner. Having made certain that no one was at home, Margarita opened the door onto the stairs and checked whether the card was there. The card was in its place; Margarita had come to the right place.

Yes, they say that to this day the critic Latunsky turns pale when he remembers that terrible evening, and to this day pronounces the name of Berlioz with reverence. It is entirely unknown what dark and vile crime might have marked that evening—on returning from the kitchen, Margarita had a heavy hammer in her hands.

The naked and invisible flier restrained herself and reasoned with herself; her hands were trembling with impatience. Taking careful aim, Margarita struck the keys of the grand piano, and the first plaintive howl swept through the whole apartment. The entirely innocent Becker baby grand screamed frenziedly. Its keys caved in, the ivory facings flew in all directions. The instrument hummed, howled, wheezed, jangled. With the sound of a revolver shot, the polished lid split under a blow of the hammer. Breathing heavily, Margarita tore and mangled the strings with the hammer. At last, tired out, she fell back and plumped into an armchair to catch her breath.
In the bathroom the water was roaring terribly, and in the kitchen too. “I think it’s already started flowing onto the floor...” thought Margarita, and added aloud:
“No time to sit about, though.”

A stream was already running from the kitchen into the corridor. Splashing through the water with her bare feet, Margarita carried water by the bucketful from the kitchen into the critic’s study and poured it into the drawers of the desk. Then, after smashing the doors of the bookcase in that same study with the hammer, she rushed into the bedroom. Breaking the mirrored wardrobe, she dragged the critic’s suit out of it and drowned it in the bathtub. A full inkwell of ink, which she had grabbed in the study, she poured out onto the plumply made-up double bed in the bedroom. The destruction she was wreaking gave her a burning delight, but all the while it seemed to her that the results were somehow paltry. So she began doing whatever came to hand. She smashed the pots of rubber plants in the room where the piano stood. Without finishing that, she went back to the bedroom and slashed the sheets with a kitchen knife and smashed the framed photographs under glass. She felt no tiredness; only the sweat ran down her in streams.

Meanwhile, in apartment No. 82, below Latunsky’s apartment, the housemaid of the dramatist Kvant was drinking tea in the kitchen, puzzled by the crashing, running about and jingling that came from above. Raising her head to the ceiling, she suddenly saw that before her very eyes it was changing its white color to a deathly bluish one. The patch was spreading before her eyes, and suddenly drops swelled on it. For about two minutes the housemaid sat marveling at this phenomenon, until at last real rain began coming from the ceiling and drumming on the floor. At this she jumped up and put a basin under the streams, which did not help in the least, since the rain spread and began flooding both the gas stove and the table with the dishes. Then, with a cry, Kvant’s housemaid ran out of the apartment onto the stairs, and at once the ringing began at Latunsky’s door.
“Well, now they’ve started ringing... Time to get going,” said Margarita. She sat on the brush, listening as a woman’s voice shouted through the keyhole:
“Open up, open up! Dusya, open up! Is it your water running? We’re flooded.”

Margarita rose a meter into the air and struck the chandelier. Two bulbs burst, and pendants flew in all directions. The shouting at the keyhole stopped; on the stairs came the sound of running feet. Margarita floated out of the window, found herself outside it, swung without much force and struck the glass with the hammer. It sobbed, and down the marble-faced wall the fragments ran in a cascade. Margarita moved on to the next window. Far below, people began running about on the pavement; of the two cars standing at the entrance, one hooted and drove off.

Having finished with Latunsky’s windows, Margarita floated over to the neighboring apartment. The blows came more often; the lane filled with ringing and crashing. The doorman ran out of the first entrance, looked up, hesitated a little, evidently not working out at once what he ought to do, stuck a whistle in his mouth and began whistling furiously. With particular zest, to the sound of this whistle, Margarita smashed the last pane on the eighth floor, went down to the seventh, and began demolishing the panes there.

Worn out by long idleness behind the glass doors of the entrance, the doorman put his whole soul into the whistling, and what’s more followed Margarita precisely, as if accompanying her. In the pauses, while she flew from window to window, he gathered his breath, and at every blow of Margarita’s he puffed out his cheeks and trilled away, drilling the night air right up to the sky.

His efforts, combined with the efforts of the furious Margarita, produced great results. Panic reigned in the building. The panes that were still whole were flung open, people’s heads appeared in them and at once hid again, while the open windows, on the contrary, were shut. In the windows of the buildings opposite, against lighted backgrounds, there appeared the dark silhouettes of people trying to understand why, for no reason at all, the panes were bursting in the new Dramlit building.

In the lane people were running toward the Dramlit House, and inside it, on every staircase, people were stamping, rushing about without any rhyme or reason. Kvant’s housemaid was shouting to those running down the stairs that they had been flooded, and she was soon joined by Khustov’s housemaid from apartment No. 80, which was below Kvant’s apartment. At the Khustovs’ it had come pouring down from the ceiling in both the kitchen and the lavatory. Finally, in the Kvants’ kitchen a huge slab of plaster crashed down from the ceiling, smashing all the dirty dishes, after which there came a real downpour: from the lattice of sagging wet lath it came pouring down in buckets. Then shouting began on the stairs of the first entrance. Flying past the second-to-last window on the fourth floor, Margarita glanced into it and saw a man who, in panic, had pulled a gas mask on. Striking his pane with the hammer, Margarita frightened him, and he vanished from the room.

And unexpectedly the wild devastation stopped. Gliding down to the third floor, Margarita looked into the end window, which was covered by a light, dark little curtain. In the room a weak little lamp was burning under a shade. In a small bed with net sides sat a little boy of about four, listening fearfully. There were no grown-ups in the room. Evidently everyone had run out of the apartment.
“They’re breaking windows,” the boy said, and called: “Mama!”
No one answered, and then he said:
“Mama, I’m scared.”
Margarita drew back the little curtain and flew in at the window.
“I’m scared,” the boy repeated, and began to tremble.
“Don’t be scared, don’t be scared, little one,” said Margarita, trying to soften her criminal voice, gone hoarse in the wind. “It was some boys breaking windows.”
“With a slingshot?” asked the boy, ceasing to tremble.
“With a slingshot, with a slingshot,” Margarita confirmed. “And you go to sleep!”
“It’s Sitnik,” said the boy. “He’s got a slingshot.”
“Well, of course, it’s him!”
The boy looked slyly off somewhere to the side and asked:
“And where are you, auntie?”
“I’m not here,” answered Margarita. “I’m a dream you’re having.”
“I thought so,” said the boy.
“You lie down,” Margarita ordered, “put your hand under your cheek, and I’ll go on being your dream.”
“All right, be my dream, be my dream,” the boy agreed, and at once lay down and put his hand under his cheek.

“I’ll tell you a fairy tale,” Margarita began, and laid her hot hand on his close-cropped head. “Once upon a time there was an auntie. And she had no children, and no happiness at all, either. And so at first she cried for a long time, and then she turned wicked...” Margarita fell silent and took her hand away—the boy was asleep.

Margarita quietly laid the hammer on the windowsill and flew out of the window. There was commotion around the building. People were running about on the asphalt pavement, strewn with broken glass, shouting something. Policemen were already flickering among them. Suddenly a bell rang out, and from the Arbat a red fire engine with a ladder rolled into the lane...

But what followed no longer interested Margarita. Taking aim so as not to catch on any wire, she gripped the brush more tightly and in an instant was above the ill-fated building. The lane beneath her tilted to one side and fell away downward. In place of that one lane, a multitude of roofs appeared under Margarita’s feet, cut across at angles by glittering pathways. All of it unexpectedly slid off to the side, and the chains of lights smeared and ran together.

Margarita gave one more spurt, and then the whole multitude of roofs fell through the earth, and in its place there appeared below a lake of trembling electric lights, and this lake suddenly rose up vertically and then appeared over Margarita’s head, while the moon flashed beneath her feet. Realizing that she had turned head over heels, Margarita righted herself and, looking back, saw that the lake was gone too, and that there, behind her, only a rosy glow remained on the horizon. And it vanished a second later, and Margarita saw that she was alone with the moon, which was flying above her and to her left. Margarita’s hair had long since been standing up in a shock, and the moonlight washed over her body with a whistle. From the way two rows of sparse lights below merged into two continuous lines of fire, from the way they quickly vanished behind, Margarita guessed that she was flying at a monstrous speed, and she was amazed that she was not suffocating.

After a few seconds had passed, far below in the earthly blackness a new lake of electric light flared up and slid under the flier’s feet, but at once it spun round like a corkscrew and fell into the earth. A few seconds more—and exactly the same phenomenon.
“Cities! Cities!” Margarita shouted.
After that, two or three times, she saw beneath her some dully gleaming sabers lying in open black cases, and realized that these were rivers.

Turning her head up and to the left, the flier admired the way the moon was racing over her like a madwoman, back toward Moscow, and at the same time, strangely, standing still, so that she could distinctly see on it something mysterious and dark—whether a dragon or the Little Humpbacked Horse—its sharp muzzle turned toward the city she had left behind.

Here the thought took hold of Margarita that, in point of fact, she was driving the brush so frenziedly for nothing. That she was depriving herself of the chance to see anything properly, to drink her fill of the flight properly. Something told her that there, where she was flying, they would wait for her, and that there was no need for her to be bored by such insane speed and height.

Margarita tilted the brush bristles forward, so that its tail rose upward, and, slowing down greatly, made for the very ground. And this gliding downward, as if on an airy sled, gave her the greatest delight of all. The earth rose toward her, and in its black mass, formless until then, its secrets and charms on a moonlit night came into view. The earth came toward her, and Margarita was already bathed in the smell of greening forests. Margarita flew right over the mists of a dewy meadow, then over a pond. Beneath Margarita the frogs were singing in chorus, and somewhere in the distance, for some reason stirring her heart very much, a train was rumbling. Soon Margarita saw it. It was crawling slowly, like a caterpillar, scattering sparks into the air. Overtaking it, Margarita passed over another watery mirror, in which a second moon floated by beneath her feet, came down lower still and went on, her feet all but brushing the tops of huge pines.

A heavy noise of air being ripped apart came from behind and began to overtake Margarita. Gradually, to this noise of something flying like a shell was added a woman’s laughter, audible for many versts. Margarita looked round and saw that some complicated dark object was catching up with her. As it overtook Margarita, it took clearer and clearer shape; it became visible that someone was flying astride. And at last it took shape completely: slowing down, Natasha caught up with Margarita.

She, completely naked, with her tousled hair flying in the air, was flying astride a fat hog that clutched a briefcase in its front trotters while its hind ones furiously threshed the air. A pince-nez that had fallen off its nose, glinting now and then in the moonlight and then going dark, flew alongside the hog on its cord, and a hat kept sliding down over the hog’s eyes. Looking closely, Margarita recognized Nikolai Ivanovich in the hog, and then her laughter thundered over the forest, mingling with Natasha’s laughter.
“Natashka!” Margarita shouted piercingly. “Did you rub yourself with the cream?”
“My darling!” answered Natasha, waking the sleeping pine forest with her yells. “My French queen, I rubbed it on his bald patch too, his too!”
“Princess!” the hog bellowed tearfully, galloping along with his rider.

“My darling! Margarita Nikolayevna!” shouted Natasha, galloping alongside Margarita. “I confess, I took the cream! We want to live and fly too, you know! Forgive me, my sovereign lady, but I’m not going back, not for anything will I go back! Ah, it’s wonderful, Margarita Nikolayevna!.. He proposed to me”—Natasha began jabbing her finger into the neck of the embarrassed, puffing hog—“proposed! What did you call me, eh?” she shouted, bending down to the hog’s ear.
“Goddess!” he howled. “I can’t fly so fast! I may lose important papers. Natalya Prokofyevna, I protest.”
“Oh, to the devil with you and your papers!” shouted Natasha, laughing insolently.
“What are you saying, Natalya Prokofyevna! Somebody will hear us!” the hog bellowed imploringly.
Flying at a gallop beside Margarita, Natasha, laughing, told her what had happened in the house after Margarita Nikolayevna flew away over the gate.

Natasha confessed that, without touching any more of the things she had been given, she had thrown off her clothes, rushed to the cream and immediately rubbed herself with it. And the same thing happened to her as to her mistress. While Natasha, laughing with joy, was reveling in her magical beauty before the mirror, the door opened and Nikolai Ivanovich appeared before Natasha. He was agitated; in his hands he held Margarita Nikolayevna’s chemise and his own hat and briefcase. On seeing Natasha, Nikolai Ivanovich was struck dumb. Having mastered himself somewhat, red as a lobster all over, he announced that he had considered it his duty to pick up the little chemise and bring it back in person...

“The things he said, the scoundrel!” Natasha squealed and laughed. “The things he said, what he tried to lure me into! What money he promised! He said Klavdia Petrovna would never find out. What, are you going to say I’m lying?” Natasha shouted to the hog, and he only turned his snout away in embarrassment.

Getting playful in the bedroom, Natasha dabbed Nikolai Ivanovich with the cream, and was herself dumbfounded with astonishment. The respectable downstairs tenant’s face shrank into a snout, and his hands and feet turned out to have little trotters. Glancing at himself in the mirror, Nikolai Ivanovich let out a desperate, wild howl, but it was already too late. A few seconds later, saddled, he was flying off somewhere to the devil, out of Moscow, sobbing with grief.

“I demand the restoration of my normal appearance!” the hog suddenly wheezed and grunted, half frenzied, half imploring. “I have no intention of flying to an unlawful gathering! Margarita Nikolayevna, you are obliged to restrain your housemaid!”
“Oh, so now I’m your housemaid, am I? A housemaid?” cried Natasha, pinching the hog’s ear. “And before I was a goddess? What did you call me?”
“Venus!” the hog answered tearfully, flying over a stream that babbled among the stones and brushing the hazel bushes with a rustle of his trotters.

“Venus! Venus!” Natasha shouted triumphantly, one hand on her hip and the other stretched out toward the moon. “Margarita! Queen! Plead for me, so that they let me stay a witch! They’ll do anything for you; you’ve been given power!”
And Margarita responded:
“Very well, I promise.”

“Thank you!” shouted Natasha, and suddenly cried out sharply and somehow wistfully: “Hey! Hey! Faster! Faster! Come on, put on some speed!” She squeezed with her heels the hog’s flanks, which had grown thinner in the insane race, and he shot forward so that the air was ripped apart again, and a moment later Natasha could be seen far ahead as a black dot, and then she vanished altogether, and the noise of her flight melted away.

Margarita flew on slowly, as before, over a deserted and unknown country, over hills strewn with scattered boulders lying among solitary huge pines. Margarita flew and thought that she was probably somewhere very far from Moscow. The brush was flying no longer over the tops of the pines but between their trunks, silvered on one side by the moon. The light shadow of the flier slid along the ground ahead—now the moon was shining on Margarita’s back.

Margarita sensed the nearness of water and guessed that her goal was close. The pines parted, and Margarita rode quietly through the air up to a chalk cliff. Beyond this cliff, below, in shadow, lay a river. Mist hung and clung to the bushes at the foot of the sheer cliff, while the opposite bank was flat and low-lying. On it, under a solitary clump of some spreading trees, a little campfire flickered, and some small moving figures could be seen. It seemed to Margarita that some buzzing, jolly little music was coming from there. Beyond, as far as the eye could see, there was no sign of any dwelling or of people on the silvered plain.

Margarita leaped down from the cliff and quickly descended to the water. The water beckoned her after the race through the air. Flinging the brush aside, she took a run and dived headfirst into the water. Her light body pierced the water like an arrow, and a column of water was thrown up almost to the moon itself. The water turned out to be warm, as in a bathhouse, and, surfacing from the depths, Margarita swam to her heart’s content in complete solitude, at night, in that river.
There was no one near Margarita, but a little further on, beyond the bushes, there was splashing and snorting; someone was bathing there too.

Margarita ran out onto the bank. Her body was glowing after the swim. She felt no tiredness at all and danced joyfully on the damp grass. Suddenly she stopped dancing and pricked up her ears. The snorting came nearer, and from behind the willow bushes there climbed out a naked fat man in a black silk top hat tilted onto the back of his head. The soles of his feet were covered in silty mud, so that it looked as though the bather was wearing black boots. Judging by the way he puffed and hiccuped, he was fairly drunk, which, by the way, was confirmed by the fact that the river suddenly began to give off a smell of cognac.
On seeing Margarita, the fat man began to peer at her, and then yelled joyfully:
“What’s this? Is it she I see? Claudine, why, it’s you, the merry widow! And you’re here too?” And with that he came forward to greet her.
Margarita stepped back and answered with dignity:

“Go to the devil’s mother. What sort of Claudine am I to you? You watch who you’re talking to.” And, after thinking for a moment, she added to her speech a long unprintable curse. All this had a sobering effect on the frivolous fat man.

“Oh!” he exclaimed quietly, and gave a start. “Forgive me graciously, radiant Queen Margot! I mistook you for someone else. It’s the cognac to blame, damn it!” The fat man went down on one knee, held his top hat out to the side, made a bow and began jabbering, mixing Russian phrases with French ones, some nonsense about the bloody wedding of his friend Hessar in Paris, and about the cognac, and about how crushed he was by his sad mistake.
“You might put some trousers on, you son of a bitch,” said Margarita, softening.

The fat man grinned joyfully, seeing that Margarita was not angry, and announced rapturously that he found himself without trousers at the present moment only because he had absentmindedly left them on the river Yenisei, where he had been bathing just before, but that he would fly there at once, since it was only a stone’s throw away, and then, commending himself to her favor and protection, he began backing away and went on backing until he slipped and fell flat on his back into the water. But even as he fell, he kept on his face, framed by small side-whiskers, a smile of rapture and devotion.

Margarita, for her part, gave a piercing whistle and, mounting the brush that flew up to her, crossed over the river to the opposite bank. The shadow of the chalk hill did not reach here, and the whole bank was flooded with moonlight.

As soon as Margarita touched the damp grass, the music under the willows struck up louder, and a sheaf of sparks flew up more merrily from the fire. Under the branches of the willows, strewn with tender, fluffy catkins visible in the moonlight, sat two rows of fat-faced frogs, puffing themselves up like rubber, playing a bravura march on wooden pipes. Glowing pieces of rotten wood hung on willow twigs in front of the musicians, lighting up the music, and the restless light from the fire played on the frogs’ faces.

The march was being played in Margarita’s honor. The reception given her was of the most solemn kind. Transparent water nymphs stopped their round dance above the river and waved waterweed at Margarita, and over the deserted greenish bank their greetings moaned, audible far away. Naked witches, leaping out from behind the willows, lined up in a row and began curtsying and bowing courtly bows. Someone goat-legged flew up and pressed his lips to her hand, spread silk out on the grass, inquired whether the queen had enjoyed her bathe, and invited her to lie down and rest.

Margarita did just that. The goat-legged one brought her a glass of champagne; she drank it, and her heart was warmed at once. On inquiring where Natasha was, she received the answer that Natasha had already bathed and had flown on ahead on her hog to Moscow, to give warning that Margarita would soon be there and to help prepare her attire.

Margarita’s short stay under the willows was marked by one episode. A whistle sounded in the air, and a black body, clearly having missed its mark, came crashing down into the water. A few moments later there stood before Margarita that same side-whiskered fat man who had introduced himself so unsuccessfully on the other bank. He had evidently managed to dash off to the Yenisei, for he was in full evening dress, but wet from head to foot. The cognac had let him down a second time: landing, he had ended up in the water after all. But he had not lost his smile even in this sad situation, and the laughing Margarita admitted him to kiss her hand.

Then everyone began to get ready to leave. The water nymphs finished dancing their dance in the moonlight and melted into it. The goat-legged one respectfully inquired of Margarita what she had come to the river on. Learning that she had arrived astride a brush, he said:

“Oh, but why, that’s uncomfortable.” In a twinkling he rigged up some suspicious-looking telephone out of two twigs and demanded of someone that a car be sent this very minute, which was indeed done in one minute. A dun-colored open car came crashing down onto the island, only in the driver’s seat sat not a driver of the usual kind but a black, long-nosed rook in an oilcloth cap and gauntlets. The little island was emptying. The witches who had flown away dissolved in the blaze of moonlight. The fire was burning out, and the embers were being covered over with gray ash.

The side-whiskered man and the goat-legged one helped Margarita in, and she sank onto the wide back seat. The car howled, leaped and rose almost to the moon itself; the island vanished, the river vanished, and Margarita sped away to Moscow.

chapters.title: 22. By Candlelight
paragraphs: The even hum of the car flying high above the earth lulled Margarita, and the moonlight warmed her pleasantly. Closing her eyes, she gave her face up to the wind and thought with a kind of sadness of the unknown riverbank she had left behind, which, she felt, she would never see again. After all the sorcery and wonders of that evening she had already guessed whom exactly she was being taken to visit, but this did not frighten her. The hope that there she would succeed in getting her happiness back had made her fearless. However, she did not get to dream about this happiness in the car for long. Whether the rook knew his business well or the car was a good one, at any rate Margarita soon opened her eyes and saw beneath her not the darkness of the forest but the trembling lake of Moscow’s lights. The black bird-chauffeur unscrewed the right front wheel in midflight and then landed the car in some utterly deserted cemetery in the Dorogomilovo district.

Having set down Margarita, who asked no questions, beside one of the tombstones together with her brush, the rook started the car and sent it straight into the ravine beyond the cemetery. Into it the car crashed with a roar, and there it perished. The rook saluted respectfully, sat astride the wheel and flew away.

At once a black cloak appeared from behind one of the monuments. A fang flashed in the moonlight, and Margarita recognized Azazello. With a gesture he invited Margarita to sit on the brush, leaped onto a long rapier himself, both soared up and, noticed by no one, a few seconds later landed by building No. 302-bis on Sadovaya Street.

As the companions, carrying the brush and the rapier under their arms, passed through the gateway, Margarita noticed a man languishing in it in a cap and high boots, evidently waiting for someone. Light as Azazello’s and Margarita’s steps were, the solitary man heard them and twitched uneasily, not understanding who was making them.

A second man, astonishingly like the first, they met at the sixth entrance. And again the same story was repeated. Footsteps... The man turned round uneasily and frowned. But when the door opened and closed, he rushed after the invisible people coming in, looked into the entrance, but of course saw nothing.

A third, an exact copy of the second and therefore of the first as well, was on duty on the third-floor landing. He was smoking strong cigarettes, and Margarita had a fit of coughing as she passed him. The smoker, as if he had been pricked, jumped up from the bench he was sitting on, began looking round uneasily, went over to the banister and looked down. Margarita and her escort were by this time already at the door of apartment No. 50. They did not ring; Azazello noiselessly opened the door with his own key.

The first thing that struck Margarita was the darkness into which she had come. It was as dark as a dungeon, so that she involuntarily clutched at Azazello’s cloak, afraid of stumbling. But then, far off and high up, the flame of some little icon lamp began to flicker and to come closer. As they walked, Azazello took the brush from under Margarita’s arm, and it vanished without a sound into the darkness. Then they began climbing some broad steps, and it began to seem to Margarita that there would be no end to them. She was struck that the hall of an ordinary Moscow apartment could contain this extraordinary staircase, invisible but palpably felt, and endless. But the climb came to an end, and Margarita realized that she was standing on a landing. The little flame came right up close, and Margarita saw the lit face of a man, long and black, holding this very lamp in his hand. Those who had already had the misfortune in these days to cross his path would, of course, even in this feeble light from the lamp’s little tongue of flame, have recognized him at once. It was Koroviev, also known as Fagot.

True, Koroviev’s appearance had greatly changed. The flickering flame was reflected not in the cracked pince-nez, which ought long since to have been thrown on the rubbish heap, but in a monocle—also cracked, it is true. The little mustache on his insolent face was curled and pomaded, and Koroviev’s blackness was explained very simply: he was in evening dress. Only his chest showed white.

Magician, choirmaster, sorcerer, interpreter, or the devil knows what in reality—in a word, Koroviev—bowed and, sweeping the lamp widely through the air, invited Margarita to follow him. Azazello vanished.

“An astonishingly strange evening,” thought Margarita. “I expected anything but this! Has their electricity gone off, or what? But the most astonishing thing is the size of this place. How can all of this squeeze into a Moscow apartment? It simply and plainly can’t!”

Little as Koroviev’s lamp gave in the way of light, Margarita realized that she was in a completely boundless hall, with a colonnade into the bargain, dark and, at first impression, endless. Beside some little sofa Koroviev stopped, set his lamp down on some pedestal, invited Margarita with a gesture to sit down, and himself took up a picturesque pose beside it, leaning his elbow on the pedestal.

“Allow me to introduce myself to you,” Koroviev creaked. “Koroviev. Are you surprised that there is no light? Economy, as you no doubt thought? No-no-no! May the first executioner who comes along—say, one of those who, a little later today, will have the honor of kissing your knee—chop my head off on this very pedestal if that is so! It is simply that messire does not like electric light, and we shall turn it on at the very last moment. And then, believe me, there will be no shortage of it. It might even be better, perhaps, if there were rather less of it.”
Margarita liked Koroviev, and his crackling chatter had a calming effect on her.
“No,” answered Margarita, “what astonishes me most of all is where all this fits.” She swept her hand around, thereby emphasizing the boundlessness of the hall.
Koroviev smirked sweetly, which made the shadows stir in the folds beside his nose.

“The simplest thing of all!” he answered. “For those well acquainted with the fifth dimension, it costs nothing to push a place out to any desired limits. I will tell you more, esteemed madam: to the devil knows what limits! I have, by the way,” Koroviev chattered on, “known people who had no notion whatever, not only of the fifth dimension, but of anything at all, and who nonetheless performed the most perfect miracles when it came to enlarging their premises. So, for instance, one city dweller, so I was told, having received a three-room apartment on Zemlyanoy Val, without any fifth dimension or other things that drive the mind out of its wits, instantly turned it into a four-room apartment by dividing one of the rooms in half with a partition.

“Thereupon he exchanged this one for two separate apartments in different districts of Moscow—one of three rooms and the other of two. You must agree that there were now five. The three-room one he exchanged for two separate ones of two rooms each and became the owner, as you can see for yourself, of six rooms, scattered, it is true, in total disorder all over Moscow. He was just about to perform his last and most brilliant volte, by placing an advertisement in the newspaper that he was exchanging six rooms in different districts of Moscow for one five-room apartment on Zemlyanoy Val, when his activity was brought to an end, for reasons beyond his control. It is possible that he has some room or other now, but only, I venture to assure you, not in Moscow. There you have it, madam, what a sly operator, and you’re pleased to talk about the fifth dimension!”

Although Margarita had not talked about the fifth dimension at all—it was Koroviev himself who had talked about it—she laughed merrily on hearing the story of the adventures of the apartment schemer. Koroviev went on:
“But to business, to business, Margarita Nikolayevna. You are a very intelligent woman and have, of course, already guessed who our host is.”
Margarita’s heart thumped, and she nodded.

“Well, there you are, there you are,” Koroviev was saying. “We are enemies of all reticence and mystery. Every year messire gives one ball. It is called the spring ball of the full moon, or the ball of the hundred kings. The crowds!..” Here Koroviev clutched his cheek, as if he had a toothache. “However, I hope you will see that for yourself. And so: messire is a bachelor, as you of course understand yourself. But a hostess is needed”—Koroviev spread his hands—“you must agree yourself, without a hostess...”
Margarita listened to Koroviev, trying not to miss a single word; beneath her heart she felt cold, and the hope of happiness made her head spin.

“A tradition has become established,” Koroviev went on, “that the hostess of the ball must, firstly, without fail bear the name of Margarita, and secondly, she must be a native of the place.
